summary: Publishes the information needed to build interoperable applications that use the OpenPGP message format for encrypting and signing data such as email. It is a proposed standard that was replaced by RFC 4880.

eli5.summary: It is the rule book for sending secret and signed messages, so programs from different makers can unlock each other's secret letters.

questions: what is ascii armor in pgp
subtitle: The packet formats that let different programs encrypt, sign and exchange OpenPGP data.

tldr.problem: PGP software from different makers needed one agreed way to write down encrypted messages, signatures and keys so they could read each other's output.
tldr.mechanism: OpenPGP splits everything into tagged packets: session-key packets, signature packets, key packets, compressed and encrypted data packets. Radix-64 'ASCII armor' turns the binary stream into printable text for channels that cannot carry raw bytes.
tldr.outcome: It was a Proposed Standard from November 1998 and has been obsoleted by RFC 4880, which is the version to read today.

today: RFC 2440 was a Proposed Standard published in November 1998 and has been obsoleted by RFC 4880, which should be used instead.

sections.title: What OpenPGP Defines
sections.content:
RFC 2440 describes the message-exchange packet formats that OpenPGP uses for encryption, decryption, signing and key management. It builds on RFC 1991, 'PGP Message Exchange Formats'.

The RFC defines OpenPGP as security software that uses PGP 5.x as its basis. PGP 2.6.x, in contrast, used only RSA, MD5 and IDEA, and PGP 5.x has new formats that correct a number of problems in that design.

An IESG note at the top points out that the document defines many tag values but no procedure for adding new ones. New tag values, such as new encryption algorithms, are to be sent to the IESG Security Area Directors, because new features can interact with old ones in ways that reduce overall security.
sections.eli5: OpenPGP is a shared set of rules for scrambling and signing messages, so programs built by different people can still understand each other.

sections.title: How Encryption, Signing and Armor Work
sections.content:
OpenPGP combines digital signatures, encryption, compression and radix-64 conversion. For public-key encryption, the sender generates a random session key for each message, encrypts the message with it, and encrypts the session key to each recipient's public key. The encrypted session keys start the message. The receiver decrypts the session key with the private key, then decrypts the message. A passphrase can be used instead, or in addition.

To sign, the sender hashes the message and creates a signature from the hash with the private key. When both services are used, the signature is made first, then the message plus signature is encrypted. Implementations MAY compress after signing but before encryption.

Binary output can be turned into Radix-64 (ASCII Armor) for channels that are not safe for raw bytes. It is MIME base64 plus a 24-bit CRC written as four characters after an equals sign. Implementations SHOULD provide it. The RFC also defines a cleartext signature framework that keeps signed text readable, starting with the line -----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----, with lines beginning with a dash escaped.
sections.eli5: You lock the message with a one-time key, then lock that key inside a box only your friend can open. Signing is like stamping the letter with a seal only you own.

sections.title: Data Elements and String-to-Key
sections.content:
Scalar numbers are unsigned and big-endian. A Multi-Precision Integer (MPI) is a two-octet bit length followed by the octets of the number, so the octets 00 01 01 are an MPI with the value 1. A Key ID is an eight-octet value that identifies a key, and implementations SHOULD NOT assume Key IDs are unique. Time fields are four-octet counts of seconds since 1 January 1970 UTC, and text defaults to UTF-8.

A string-to-key (S2K) specifier turns a passphrase into a key. There are three types: simple (type 0x00, just hashes the passphrase), salted (0x01, adds an 8-octet salt) and iterated and salted (0x03, hashes the salt and passphrase repeatedly up to a coded octet count). The RFC says implementations SHOULD use salted or iterated-and-salted S2K because simple S2K is more vulnerable to dictionary attacks.
sections.eli5: A passphrase is turned into a real key by mixing it with some random salt and stirring many times, so a thief cannot just try a list of common words.

sections.title: Packets and Their Tags
sections.content:
An OpenPGP message, keyring or certificate is a series of packets. Each has a header and a body. The first header octet is the packet tag: bit 7 is always one, and bit 6 says whether the new packet format is used. Old-format packets carry a four-bit content tag and a length type, while new-format packets carry a six-bit tag. New-format lengths can be one, two or five octets, or use partial body lengths to stream data of unknown size.

Packets can contain other packets: a compressed data packet, once uncompressed, holds more OpenPGP packets. A message is built from rules such as: zero or more session-key packets, then a symmetrically encrypted data packet. A signed message is a signature packet followed by a message, or a one-pass signature packet, the message and the matching signature. Detached signatures are simply a signature packet stored separately from the data.

Key IDs and fingerprints depend on key version. A V4 fingerprint is the 160-bit SHA-1 hash of the public key packet, and the key ID is the low-order 64 bits of it.
sections.eli5: Everything is cut into small labelled parcels. The label says what is inside, so the receiving program knows whether it is a key, a signature or the secret message.

sections.title: Algorithms and Required Support
sections.content:
The RFC lists numeric IDs for algorithms but says the tables are not exhaustive, and an implementation MAY implement others. Implementations MUST implement DSA for signatures and Elgamal for encryption, and SHOULD implement RSA. For symmetric ciphers they MUST implement Triple-DES and SHOULD implement IDEA and CAST5. They MUST implement SHA-1 and SHOULD implement MD5, and they MUST implement uncompressed data and SHOULD implement ZIP.

The RFC reserves AES identifiers (7, 8 and 9 for 128, 192 and 256-bit keys) but does not make AES a supported cipher in this document.
sections.eli5: Everyone has to know a few standard locks and stamps so that any two programs can find one they both understand.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC tells readers to check current literature in case an algorithm has been found vulnerable. It notes that MD5 has weaknesses that lead some people to deprecate it in favour of SHA-1, and that many designers think using one key for both encryption and signing is a bad idea, which was a motivation for the V4 key format with separate keys.

DSA is sensitive to the quality of its hash: a broken hash can leak the secret key, not only allow forgery. Random numbers need an appropriate entropy source. Some algorithms, such as CAST5, have been analyzed less than Triple-DES, and some technologies may be subject to government control in some countries.
sections.eli5: A lock is only as good as its weakest part, so pick strong parts and keep your keys to yourself.

items.desc: Binds a public key to some data.

items.desc: Session key protected by a passphrase-derived key.
